prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the gait disorder solely to lumbar spinal stenosis: it has no claudicant pattern and improved after CSF removal
Do not withhold shunt referral because the callosal angle is above 90 degrees or DESH is absent, when the tap test is positive
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 20% in TUG at 24 hours, the supportive MRI (Evans index 0.32 with temporal horn enlargement) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Replace vitamin B12 and recheck MMA, as a possible contributor to gait and cognition; the deficiency is attributable to long-term metformin, which can continue
Counsel that shunting is expected to improve the gait more than the proximal weakness and distal sensory loss from neuropathy and lumbar stenosis, which did not change after the tap

avoided_actions.rationale: There are no episodes of altered awareness, so an EEG cannot inform this gait-predominant syndrome.
No syncope or palpitations are reported; an ECG does not bear on the gait or cognitive decline.
No cardioembolic or syncopal question exists, and the MRI shows no infarct.
MRI is available and measures the ventricles, temporal horns and callosal angle better than CT.
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or palpitations.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test; nothing here points to a neurodegenerative copathology.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
A 12-month afebrile course with normal CSF cells gives no reason for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic small-vessel disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 white matter change can cause a similar gait and executive slowing and may coexist, but the ventricles and temporal horns are enlarged and the gait improved 20% after CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Lumbar spinal stenosis as the cause of the gait disorder
differential.key_features: The stenosis is real and stable on MRI, but the gait has no positional or claudicant pattern and improved after CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Peripheral neuropathy (diabetic, vitamin B12 deficiency) as the cause of the gait disorder
differential.key_features: Distal sensory loss and absent ankle reflexes are present, but neuropathy gives a sensory ataxic gait, not a short-stepped low-clearance gait that improves after CSF removal.
No rest tremor, asymmetric rigidity or upper limb bradykinesia; the gait disorder is lower-body and responded to CSF removal.
The MoCA profile is attentional and executive with cueing benefit and the hippocampi are only mildly reduced (MTA 1), not an amnestic hippocampal pattern.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Temporal horns are enlarged out of proportion to the hippocampi without proportionate sulcal widening, and the gait responded to the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury, intracranial haemorrhage or meningitis in the history, and no haemosiderin on SWI.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH (Relkin 2005) needs an insidious, progressive gait disturbance over at least 3 to 6 months after age 40 with cognitive impairment or urinary symptoms; the full triad is not required. Here gait, cognition and urgency progressed over 12 months with no antecedent event.

Imaging needs ventricular enlargement (Evans index greater than 0.3) not entirely due to atrophy, no obstruction, and at least one supportive feature: Evans 0.32 with temporal horn enlargement out of proportion to the hippocampi qualifies, while the callosal angle of 91 degrees and absent DESH leave the MRI equivocal.

Opening pressure 15 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL, TUG improved 20% at 24 hours (30 to 24 s) with a concordant 10-m walk change. A 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive criterion; tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% and PPV 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005], so a negative tap would not have excluded iNPH.

Coexisting contributors are lumbar stenosis without claudication, diabetic neuropathy, vitamin B12 deficiency with raised MMA on metformin and Fazekas 2 small-vessel disease; they explain the residual weakness and sensory loss, not the tap-responsive gait.
Management is neurosurgical referral for a shunt with a programmable valve (AAN: possibly effective) and vitamin B12 replacement.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lumbar stenosis gives position-dependent neurogenic claudication; this gait has no positional pattern, improved after CSF removal, and the lumbar MRI is unchanged.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait limitation is attributed solely to lumbar stenosis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Distal sensory neuropathy (diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency) adds sensory imbalance but does not produce a short-stepped, low-clearance gait that improves after CSF removal.
red_herrings.data_point: Reduced vibration and light touch in both feet to the ankles
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait disorder is attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Moderate iNPH with competing contributors: lumbar stenosis, poorly controlled diabetes with neuropathy, metformin-associated vitamin B12 deficiency and Fazekas 2 white matter disease; equivocal imaging (Evans 0.32 with enlarged temporal horns, callosal angle 91 degrees, no DESH) makes the tap test decisive.

patient.history_present_illness: A 67-year-old right-handed woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity and lumbar spinal stenosis was admitted for evaluation, referred by her outpatient neurologist for progressive gait difficulty and memory decline. A brain MRI obtained 2 months ago at an outside facility to evaluate cognitive concerns was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. Over 12 months she has developed a progressive gait disorder that she and her family attributed to her known lumbar spinal stenosis. Her spine surgeon noted that the gait does not follow the pattern of neurogenic claudication: it does not worsen with standing or walking and does not ease with sitting or bending forward. Over the same period she has had increasing difficulty remembering appointments and managing her medications, and her daughter now fills her pill box. Her endocrinologist documents poor glycaemic control. She reports worsening urinary urgency with urge incontinence over the past 6 months, on a background of milder urgency previously attributed to diabetic bladder dysfunction. There is no history of head injury, intracranial haemorrhage or meningitis.

neurological_exam.additional: No clonus. Lumbar range of motion limited.
neurological_exam.gait: Short-stepped, wide-based, shuffling gait with reduced step height and turns in several small steps. It does not worsen with prolonged walking or ease with forward flexion. Obesity limits the assessment.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented, attentive, slowed responses; formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal upper limb strength. Mild proximal lower limb weakness 4+/5 bilaterally. Mildly increased lower limb tone with paratonia.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Patellar reflexes reduced (1+) bilaterally. Achilles reflexes absent bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced vibration and light touch in both feet to the ankles. No saddle anaesthesia.
